title: How DNS Works: Why Changing to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8) Speeds Up Your Internet
html:
Have you ever noticed that when you click a link on your smartphone or laptop, there is a slight 1-to-2 second pause where the browser displays "Resolving host..." before the webpage starts loading? Once the connection begins, content streams smoothly—but that initial hesitation happens on almost every new website you visit.

Last updated: 25 Nov 2026. This comprehensive networking guide explains how the Domain Name System (DNS) works, why your default telecom provider's DNS is slow and monitors your browsing history, and how switching to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), Google (8.8.8.8), or AdGuard can make your internet feel noticeably faster.

What Is DNS and Why Does Every Webpage Depend on It?

Computers and servers communicating across the global internet do not understand human language or website names like trendswheel.com or google.com. They navigate exclusively using numerical IP (Internet Protocol) addresses (such as 142.250.190.46 for IPv4 or 2606:4700::6810:84e5 for IPv6).

The Domain Name System (DNS) is the phonebook of the internet. Every time you tap a link or enter a URL in your browser:

  1. Your device pauses and queries a DNS recursive resolver server: "What is the numerical IP address for this website?"
  2. The DNS server searches its cache or contacts authoritative root name servers.
  3. The DNS server responds with the IP address.
  4. Only then can your browser initiate the HTTPS handshake and fetch the webpage.

A single modern news article or blog page often contains content loaded from 15 to 30 different domain names (fonts, CSS styles, images, analytics, and video embeds). That means loading one webpage can trigger dozens of separate DNS lookup requests.

The 3 Major Problems with Your ISP's Default DNS

When you set up home Wi-Fi or turn on mobile data, your phone automatically uses the default DNS servers operated by your telecom provider (Jio, Airtel, Vi, Vodafone, Comcast, etc.). This creates three major issues:

  1. Sluggish Response Times (High Lookup Latency): ISP DNS servers are often poorly optimized and geographically centralized. A lookup on a congested ISP resolver can take 65ms to 120ms per query, compared to just 12ms to 15ms on Cloudflare's Anycast edge network.
  2. Unencrypted Plaintext Snooping: Traditional DNS queries travel over port 53 in unencrypted plaintext. Even if a website uses secure HTTPS encryption, your ISP sees every single domain name you look up and logs your browsing history, often selling anonymized telemetry to marketing networks.
  3. Arbitrary Censorship and DNS Hijacking: ISPs frequently implement government blocking orders or redirect mistyped URLs to their own ad-heavy "Search Assistance" landing pages.

How to Change Your DNS in 60 Seconds

1. On Android (Private DNS - Recommended):

  1. Open Settings → Network & internet (or Connection & sharing).
  2. Tap Private DNS.
  3. Select Private DNS provider hostname and enter either:
    • one.one.one.one (for Cloudflare's ultra-fast encrypted DNS).
    • dns.adguard-dns.com (for automatic ad and tracker blocking across all apps and games!).
  4. Tap Save. All DNS queries on both mobile data and Wi-Fi are now encrypted via DNS-over-TLS (DoT).

2. On Windows 11:

  1. Go to Settings → Network & internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet) → Hardware properties.
  2. Next to DNS server assignment, click Edit → select Manual.
  3. Toggle IPv4 ON.
  4. Preferred DNS: 1.1.1.1. Alternate DNS: 1.0.0.1.
  5. Set DNS over HTTPS to On (automatic template) to enable full encryption.

3. On Your Home Wi-Fi Router:

Log into your home router's admin panel (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1), navigate to DHCP / WAN Settings, and enter 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1 as primary and secondary DNS. Every smart TV, gaming console, and phone connected to your home Wi-Fi will instantly benefit from faster lookup speeds without configuring individual devices.

faq.title: Will changing DNS increase my raw internet download speed?
faq.description: DNS does not change your maximum bandwidth cap (e.g. 100 Mbps stays 100 Mbps). However, it drastically cuts the initial lookup latency (from 100ms down to 12ms) whenever you click a link, making webpages snap open noticeably faster.

faq.title: Which is faster: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 or Google 8.8.8.8?
faq.description: Independent global DNS monitoring benchmarks consistently rank Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 as the fastest public DNS resolver worldwide due to its 310+ Anycast edge datacenter network.

faq.title: Can changing DNS block mobile ads without installing apps?
faq.description: Yes. Setting Android Private DNS to dns.adguard-dns.com routes DNS lookups through ad-blocking filters, blocking ads inside browser pages, mobile apps, and games system-wide.
